Use `{type: "thinking_turns", value: N}` where N must be > 0 to keep the last N turns, or `"all"` to keep all thinking blocks. Opus 4.5+ and Sonnet 4.6+: all turns. Earlier Opus/Sonnet and all Haiku: last turn only. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options-for-thinking-block-clearing
- [parameter] `trigger`: Default=100,000 input tokens; Description=Defines when the context editing strategy activates. Once the prompt exceeds this threshold, clearing begins. You can specify this value in either `input_tokens` or `tool_uses`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options-for-tool-result-clearing
- [parameter] `keep`: Default=3 tool uses; Description=Defines how many recent tool use/result pairs to keep after clearing occurs. The API removes the oldest tool interactions first, preserving the most recent ones. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options-for-tool-result-clearing
- [parameter] `clear_at_least`: Default=None; Description=Ensures a minimum number of tokens is cleared each time the strategy activates. If the API can't clear at least the specified amount, the strategy will not be applied. This helps determine if context clearing is worth breaking your prompt cache. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options-for-tool-result-clearing
- [parameter] `exclude_tools`: Default=None; Description=List of tool names whose tool uses and results should never be cleared. Useful for preserving important context. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options-for-tool-result-clearing
- [parameter] `clear_tool_inputs`: Default=`false`; Description=Controls whether the tool call parameters are cleared along with the tool results. By default, only the tool results are cleared while keeping Claude's original tool calls visible. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options-for-tool-result-clearing
- [parameter] `enabled`: Type=boolean; Required=Yes; Default=-; Description=Whether to enable automatic compaction — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options
- [parameter] `context_token_threshold`: Type=number; Required=No; Default=100,000; Description=Token count at which compaction triggers — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#configuration-options

- [definition] Overview — For most use cases, [server-side compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction) is the primary strategy for managing context in long-running conversations. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing#overview

## How the context window works
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows>

- [snippet] How it works: <budget:token_budget>200000</budget:token_budget> — `<budget:token_budget>200000</budget:token_budget>` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#how-it-works
- [snippet] How it works: <system_warning>Token usage: 35000/200000; 165000 remaining</system_warning> — `<system_warning>Token usage: 35000/200000; 165000 remaining</system_warning>` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#how-it-works
- [definition] How the context window works — The "context window" refers to all the text a language model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself. This is different from the large corpus of data the language model was trained on, and instead represents a "working memory" for the model. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#how-the-context-window-works
- [definition] Context window sizes by model — Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 have a 1M-token context window on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. [Claude Mythos Preview](https://anthropic.com/glasswing) also has a 1M-token context window. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#context-window-sizes-by-model
- [definition] The context window with thinking — With [thinking](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking), all input and output tokens, including thinking tokens, count toward the context window limit, with a few nuances in multi-turn situations. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#the-context-window-with-thinking
- [definition] The context window with thinking and tool use — The following diagram illustrates how tokens are managed when you combine thinking with tool use on a model that strips previous thinking blocks: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#the-context-window-with-thinking-and-tool-use
- [definition] Context awareness — Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5 have **context awareness:** these models track their remaining context window (their "token budget") throughout a conversation. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#context-awareness
- [definition] How it works — In the system prompt of every request, the API gives Claude its total context window: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#how-it-works
- [definition] Manage context with compaction — If your conversations regularly approach context window limits, use [server-side compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#manage-context-with-compaction
- [definition] Context window overflow behavior — If the input alone already exceeds the model's context window, the API returns a 400 `invalid_request_error` ("prompt is too long") on every model. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows#context-window-overflow-behavior

- [definition] Write docker-compose.yaml — The compose file pins images by SHA-256 digest, runs every container as non-root with a read-only filesystem, drops all Linux capabilities, and disables privilege escalation. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#install

- [definition] Get the tunnel token and domain from the Console — On the tunnel detail page, copy the **Domain** (it has the form `abcd1234.tunnel.anthropic.com`), then click the eye icon next to **Token** to fetch the tunnel token and use the copy icon to copy it. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#install
- [definition] Register the CA certificate in the Console — On the tunnel detail page, scroll to the **Certificates** section and click **Add certificate**. - [definition] Write the proxy config — `tunnel_domain` is **required**: the proxy uses it to strip the domain suffix from incoming hostnames before looking up the subdomain in `routes`. `routes` is a flat map from subdomain to upstream URL, not a list. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#install
- [definition] Write docker-compose.yaml — The `network_mode: "service:mcp-proxy"` setting places [cloudflared](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) in the proxy's network namespace so that `localhost:8080` inside the cloudflared container reaches the proxy. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#install
- [definition] Verify the deployment — Verify end to end by calling an [upstream MCP server](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) from Anthropic's side: see [Use the tunneled MCP… — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#verify-the-deployment
- [definition] Upgrades — Run the commands in this section from inside the `mcp-tunnel/` deployment directory. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#upgrades
- [definition] Rotate the tunnel token — With programmatic access, increment `--token-version` in the `setup` service command, set the Workload Identity Federation identifiers, mint a fresh OIDC JWT, and re-run the setup component: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#rotate-the-tunnel-token
- [definition] Certificate renewal — You're responsible for monitoring expiry and renewing the server certificate before it expires. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-compose#certificate-renewal

- [definition] Set up Workload Identity Federation for the cluster — Follow [Use WIF with Kubernetes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/wif-providers/kubernetes) to register your cluster's OIDC issuer and create a federation rule. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Configure tunnel attachment and routes — Edit `values.yaml` and set the `api.wif.*` keys with the federation rule ID and organization ID, plus a `routes` entry for each [upstream MCP server](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components): — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Review the rendered manifests — Render the chart and review the output according to your organization's vetting practices: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Get the tunnel token and domain — [Create the tunnel](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel) and [get the tunnel token from the Console](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#get-the-connection-details). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Generate a CA and server certificate — The proxy listens on plain WebSocket, with [inner TLS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) carried inside that stream using the certificate you generate here. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Create the two Secrets — The chart reads specific keys; the Secret names are configurable but the keys are not. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Configure values for manual provisioning — Edit `values.yaml` and set the following keys: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#install
- [definition] Verify the deployment — Verify end to end from Anthropic's side: use `https://<route>.<your-tunnel-domain>/<path>` in a Managed Agent session or a Messages API request, where `<route>` is a key from `gateway.config.routes` and `<path>` is whatever the upstream MCP server serves at. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#verify-the-deployment
- [definition] Restrict egress with NetworkPolicy — Ingress to the proxy pod is denied by default (`networkPolicy.ingress.enabled: true`). To additionally restrict pod egress, set `networkPolicy.egress.enabled: true` and populate `networkPolicy.egress.mcpServers` with pod label selectors or CIDR ranges that cover your upstream MCP servers. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#restrict-egress-with-networkpolicy
- [definition] Tune the proxy — Fields under `gateway.config.*` pass through to the proxy configuration file. Common adjustments include `upstream.allowed_ips`, `log_level`, and `upstream.tls`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#tune-the-proxy
- [definition] Supply your own OIDC token — By default the chart projects a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token for the setup component. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#supply-your-own-oidc-token
- [definition] Upgrades — Always pass `--version` to `helm upgrade` so you don't pull a newer chart unexpectedly. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#upgrades
- [definition] Upgrade from chart 1.x — Chart 2.0.0 moves the tunnel ID from `api.wif.tunnelId` to `tunnel.id`. Before upgrading, edit your `values.yaml`: move the `tnl_...` value to `tunnel.id` and remove `api.wif.tunnelId`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#upgrade-from-chart-1x
- [definition] Change configuration — For routine changes such as routes, replica count, or NetworkPolicy: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#change-configuration
- [definition] Rotate the tunnel token — With programmatic access, increment `tunnel.tokenVersion` in `values.yaml` and upgrade with `--set setup.force=true`. The setup component only re-runs on upgrades when forced: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#rotate-the-tunnel-token
- [definition] Certificate renewal — The chart provides automation, but you remain responsible for monitoring expiry and confirming renewal completes. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/deploy-helm#certificate-renewal

- [parameter] `max`: Description=Absolute maximum capability with no constraints on token spending. Available on Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Mythos Preview, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.; Typical use case=Tasks requiring the deepest possible reasoning and most thorough analysis — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-levels
- [parameter] `xhigh`: Description=Extended capability for long-horizon work. Available on Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 4.7, and Claude Sonnet 5.; Typical use case=Long-running agentic and coding tasks (over 30 minutes) with token budgets in the millions — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-levels
- [parameter] `high`: Description=High capability. Equivalent to not setting the parameter.; Typical use case=Complex reasoning, difficult coding problems, agentic tasks — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-levels
- [parameter] `medium`: Description=Balanced approach with moderate token savings.; Typical use case=Agentic tasks that require a balance of speed, cost, and performance — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-levels
- [parameter] `low`: Description=Most efficient. Significant token savings with some capability reduction.; Typical use case=Simpler tasks that need the best speed and lowest costs, such as subagents — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-levels
- [parameter] `low`: Efficient, but best for short, scoped tasks. Pair `low` with explicit checklists if your task has multiple sections. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-47
- [parameter] `medium`: The drop-in for the average workflow where you want good results while reducing costs. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-47
- [parameter] `high`: Advanced use cases that still need a balance of intelligence and token consumption. This is often the best balance of quality and token efficiency. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-47
- [parameter] `xhigh`: The recommended starting point for coding and agentic work, and for exploratory tasks such as repeated tool calling, detailed web search, and knowledge-base search. Expect meaningfully higher token usage than `high`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-47
- [parameter] `max`: Reserve for genuinely frontier problems. On most workloads `max` adds significant cost for relatively small quality gains, and on some structured-output or less intelligence-sensitive tasks it can lead to overthinking. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-47
- [definition] How effort works — By default, Claude uses high effort, spending as many tokens as needed for excellent results. You can raise the effort level to `max` for the absolute highest capability, or lower it to be more conservative with token usage, optimizing for speed and cost while accepting some reduction in capability. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#how-effort-works

- [definition] Recommended effort levels for Claude Sonnet 4.6 — Sonnet 4.6 defaults to `high` effort. Explicitly set effort when using Sonnet 4.6 to avoid unexpected latency: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-sonnet-46
- [definition] Recommended effort levels for Claude Opus 4.8 — The guidance for Claude Opus 4.7 also applies to Claude Opus 4.8. **Start with `xhigh` for coding and agentic use cases**, use `high` for most other intelligence-sensitive workloads, and step down to `medium` or `low` only when you've measured that the lower level holds quality on your evals. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-48
- [definition] Recommended effort levels for Claude Opus 5 — Claude Opus 5 supports all five effort levels. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-opus-5
- [definition] Recommended effort levels for Claude Fable 5 — Effort is the primary control for trading off intelligence, latency, and cost on Claude Fable 5. **Start with `high`, the default, for most tasks**, use `xhigh` for the most capability-sensitive workloads, and step down to `medium` or `low` for routine work. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#recommended-effort-levels-for-claude-fable-5
- [definition] Effort with tool use — When using tools, the effort parameter affects both the explanations around tool calls and the tool calls themselves. Lower effort levels tend to: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-with-tool-use
- [definition] Effort with thinking — The `thinking` parameter controls whether Claude thinks in [thinking blocks](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking) before answering; the `effort` parameter controls how much work Claude puts into the whole response, which in adaptive mode includes how often and how deeply… — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#effort-with-thinking
- [definition] Changing effort mid-conversation — `output_config.effort` is a request-level setting: each request carries its own value, so to run a later part of a conversation at a different effort level, set the new value on the next request. The effort level applies to the whole request. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#changing-effort-mid-conversation
- [definition] Best practices — 1. **Set effort explicitly:** The API defaults to `high`, but the right starting point depends on your model and workload. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort#best-practices

## The basic flow
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit>

- [snippet] cURL: response=$(curl --fail-with-body -sS https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages \ — `# Initial request (may be refused)` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] CLI: response=$(ant beta:messages create \ — `# Initial request (may be refused)` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] Python: client = Anthropic() — `client = Anthropic()` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] TypeScript: const client = new Anthropic(); — `const client = new Anthropic();` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] C#: var client = new AnthropicClient(); — `var client = new AnthropicClient();` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] Go: ctx := context.Background() — `ctx := context.Background()` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] Java: AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); — `AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv();` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] PHP: $client = new Client(); — `$client = new Client();` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [snippet] Ruby: client = Anthropic::Client.new — `client = Anthropic::Client.new` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [parameter] `true`: The refused request body, unchanged, plus one appended assistant message whose `content` echoes the refused response's `content`. The retry model continues the response from where the refused model stopped, and completed server tool calls are not re-executed. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#the-basic-flow
- [parameter] `false`: The refused request body, unchanged. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#the-basic-flow
- [parameter] Must match exactly: `system`, `messages`, `tools`, `tool_choice`, `thinking`, and `cache_control`, plus `output_config`, `mcp_servers`, `context_management`, and `container` when you use them — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#reference
- [parameter] May change on the retry: `model`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequences`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `stream`, `metadata`, and `service_tier` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#reference
- [definition] Opt in with the beta header — Send the request that may be refused with the `anthropic-beta: fallback-credit-2026-07-01` header. The `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` header also grants the same fields, and the earlier `fallback-credit-2026-06-01` header remains accepted and grants the same fields. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#the-basic-flow
- [definition] Read two fields from the refusal — On a refusal, `stop_details` includes two fields: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#the-basic-flow
- [definition] Build the retry — Start from the refused request body. Set `model` to the fallback model and add the token as the top-level `fallback_credit_token` parameter. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#the-basic-flow
- [definition] Send the retry with the same header — Send the retry with the same `fallback-credit-2026-07-01` beta header. The retry needs the header to redeem the token. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#the-basic-flow
- [definition] Example — The following example makes a request that may be refused and redeems the credit token on a retry against Claude Opus 4.8. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#example
- [definition] Where it works — Fallback credit is in beta on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#where-it-works
- [definition] Checking that the credit applied — The refund is visible in the retry's `usage`. Compared with what the same request would report without the token, `cache_creation_input_tokens` is lower, and `cache_read_input_tokens` is higher by the same amount. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#checking-that-the-credit-applied
- [definition] When a retry is rejected — Most retries redeem on the first attempt. When one does not, the API returns a 400 error that tells you what to try next. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#when-a-retry-is-rejected
- [definition] Continuation rejected: resend the unchanged body — If the retry that appends the assistant message is rejected with a 400 error, resend the refused request body unchanged, still with the token. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#when-a-retry-is-rejected
- [definition] Token rejected: drop the token — If the unchanged body is also rejected with a 400 error whose message names `fallback_credit_token`, retry without the token. The credit is forfeited, but the retry itself goes through. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#when-a-retry-is-rejected
- [definition] Reference — The sections below cover edge cases and the complete redemption rules. Most integrations do not need them. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fallback-credit#reference

- [parameter] `anthropic-fast-input-tokens-limit`: Maximum fast mode input tokens per minute — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [parameter] `anthropic-fast-input-tokens-remaining`: Remaining fast mode input tokens — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [parameter] `anthropic-fast-input-tokens-reset`: Time when the fast mode input token limit resets — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [parameter] `anthropic-fast-output-tokens-limit`: Maximum fast mode output tokens per minute — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [parameter] `anthropic-fast-output-tokens-remaining`: Remaining fast mode output tokens — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [parameter] `anthropic-fast-output-tokens-reset`: Time when the fast mode output token limit resets — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [definition] Supported models — Fast mode is supported on the following models: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#supported-models
- [definition] How fast mode works — Fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration. There is no change to intelligence or capabilities. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#how-fast-mode-works
- [definition] Pricing — Fast mode is priced at a multiplier on standard rates across the full context window, including requests over 200k input tokens. The following table shows fast mode pricing for the supported models: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#pricing
- [definition] Rate limits — Fast mode has a dedicated rate limit that is separate from standard Opus rate limits. When your fast mode rate limit is exceeded, the API returns a `429` error with a `retry-after` header indicating when capacity will be available. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#rate-limits
- [definition] Checking which speed was used — The response `usage` object includes a `speed` field that indicates which speed was used, either `"fast"` or `"standard"`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#checking-which-speed-was-used
- [definition] Automatic retries — When fast mode rate limits are exceeded, the API returns a `429` error with a `retry-after` header. The Anthropic SDKs automatically retry these requests up to 2 times by default (configurable with `max_retries`), waiting for the server-specified delay before each retry. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#automatic-retries
- [definition] Falling back to standard speed — This section covers an opt-in client-side fallback when fast mode is rate limited. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#falling-back-to-standard-speed

- [definition] File type support — Referencing a `file_id` in a Messages request is supported on all models that support the given file type. - [definition] How the Files API works — The Files API provides a create-once, use-many-times approach for working with files: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#how-the-files-api-works
- [definition] Uploading a file — Upload a file to be referenced in future API calls: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#uploading-a-file
- [definition] Using a file in messages — Once uploaded, reference the file by passing the `id` from the upload response as `file_id`: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#using-a-file-in-messages
- [definition] File types and content blocks — The Files API supports different file types that correspond to different content block types: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#file-types-and-content-blocks
- [definition] Working with other file formats — For file types that the `document` block doesn't support (for example, .docx and .xlsx), convert the files to plain text and include the content directly in your message. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#working-with-other-file-formats
- [definition] Downloading a file — Download files that were created by [skills](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/skills-guide) or the [code execution tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/code-execution-tool). Files you upload cannot be downloaded. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#downloading-a-file
- [definition] File expiration — To have a file expire automatically, include an `expires_in_seconds` form field when you upload it. The value is an integer number of seconds between 3,600 (1 hour) and 7,776,000 (90 days). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#file-expiration
- [definition] Audit logging — If your organization has the [Compliance API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-api) enabled, its [Activity Feed](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-activity-feed) records Files API operations made with a Claude API key or from the Claude… — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#audit-logging
- [definition] Migrate from `files-api-2025-04-14` — The Files API is out of beta and needs no beta header. Migrating off `files-api-2025-04-14` is optional: requests that still send it keep working and keep returning the beta response shapes, so an existing integration keeps working until you change it. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#migrate-from-files-api-2025-04-14
- [definition] SDK beta namespace — Starting with Python SDK 1.2.0, TypeScript SDK 0.122.0, Go SDK 1.68.0, Java SDK 2.59.0, Ruby SDK 1.67.0, and C# SDK 12.44.0, `client.beta.files` no longer sends `files-api-2025-04-14` and returns the same shapes as `client.files`, with `Beta`-prefixed type names. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#sdk-beta-namespace
- [definition] Error handling — Common errors when using the Files API include: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#error-handling
- [definition] Rate limits — File-related API calls are limited to approximately 500 requests per minute. To request a higher limit, [contact sales](mailto:sales@anthropic.com). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files#rate-limits

## The tool-use contract
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works>

- [parameter] User-defined client tools: When to use it=Custom business logic, internal APIs, proprietary data; What to expect=You handle execution and the agentic loop; Learn more=[Define tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#choosing-between-approaches
- [parameter] Anthropic-schema client tools: When to use it=Standard dev operations (bash, file editing, desktop and browser control); What to expect=You handle execution; Claude calls the tool reliably because the schema is trained-in; Learn more=[Tool reference](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#choosing-between-approaches
- [parameter] Server-executed tools: When to use it=Web search, code sandbox, web fetch; What to expect=Anthropic handles execution; you read the results instead of producing them; Learn more=[Server tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/server-tools) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#choosing-between-approaches
- [definition] The tool-use contract — Tool use is a contract between your application and the model. You specify what operations are available and what shape their inputs and outputs take; Claude determines when and how to call them. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#the-tool-use-contract
- [definition] Where tools run — The primary axis along which tools differ is where the code executes. Every tool falls into one of three buckets, and the bucket determines what your application is responsible for. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#where-tools-run
- [definition] User-defined tools (client-executed) — You write the schema, you execute the code, you return the results. This is the most common case: the vast majority of tool-use traffic is [user-defined tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools) calling into application-specific logic. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#user-defined-tools-client-executed
- [definition] Anthropic-schema tools (client-executed) — For a handful of common operations (managing scratchpad memory, running shell commands, editing files, controlling a desktop or a browser), Anthropic publishes the tool schema and your application handles execution. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#anthropic-schema-tools-client-executed
- [definition] Server-executed tools — For [`web_search`](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-search-tool), [`web_fetch`](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/web-fetch-tool), [`code_execution`](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/code-execution-tool), and… — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#server-executed-tools
- [definition] The agentic loop (client tools) — Client-executed tools (both user-defined and Anthropic-schema) require your application to drive a loop. The model can't run your code, so every tool call is a round trip: the model asks, you execute, you report back, the model continues. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#the-agentic-loop-client-tools
- [definition] The server-side loop — Server-executed tools run their own loop inside Anthropic's infrastructure. A single request from your application might trigger several web searches or code executions before a response comes back. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#the-server-side-loop
- [definition] When to use tools (and when not to) — Tool use fits when the task requires something the model can't do from text alone: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works#when-to-use-tools-and-when-not-to

## The four approaches
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context>

- [parameter] Tool search: What it reduces=Tool definitions loaded upfront; When it fits=Large toolsets (20+ tools) where most tools aren't needed every turn; Learn more=[Tool search tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#the-four-approaches
- [parameter] Programmatic tool calling: What it reduces=`tool_result` roundtrips; When it fits=Chains of tool calls that can execute as a single script; Learn more=[Programmatic tool calling](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/programmatic-tool-calling) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#the-four-approaches
- [parameter] Prompt caching: What it reduces=Token cost of repeated tool definitions; When it fits=Stable toolsets across many requests; Learn more=[Tool use with prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-use-with-prompt-caching) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#the-four-approaches
- [parameter] Context editing: What it reduces=Old `tool_result` blocks in history; When it fits=Long conversations where early results are no longer relevant; Learn more=[Context editing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#the-four-approaches
- [definition] The four approaches — Each approach targets a different source of context pressure. Pick the one that matches where your tokens are going. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#the-four-approaches
- [definition] Tool search — Tool search keeps tool definitions out of the context window until Claude asks for them. Instead of sending 50 tool schemas upfront, you send a single `tool_search` tool and let Claude discover the rest on demand. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#tool-search
- [definition] Programmatic tool calling — Programmatic tool calling collapses a sequence of tool calls into a single code block that Claude writes and Anthropic's code execution sandbox runs. Rather than five roundtrips of `tool_use` and `tool_result`, Claude emits one script that calls all five functions from within the sandbox. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#programmatic-tool-calling
- [definition] Prompt caching — Prompt caching doesn't reduce the number of tokens in context, but it reduces what you pay for them on subsequent requests. If your tool definitions are stable, cache them once and reuse the cached prefix across thousands of requests. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#prompt-caching
- [definition] Context editing — Context editing removes old `tool_result` blocks from the conversation history once they've served their purpose. A long agent loop might produce hundreds of intermediate results that were useful at the time but are now dead weight. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#context-editing
- [definition] Combining approaches — These approaches compose. A long-running agent might use tool search to keep the toolset lean, prompt caching to amortize the cost of the remaining definitions, and context editing to trim stale results as the conversation grows. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context#combining-approaches

## Prerequisites
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console>

- [parameter] The **federation rule ID** (`fdrl_...`) of the rule you selected. The rule is org-level, not stored on the tunnel; find it under **Settings > Workload identity > Rules**.: The **tunnel token**, revealed with the eye icon next to **Token** on the detail page. Treat it as a secret. See [Get the connection… — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel
- [parameter] The **organization ID** (a UUID), shown under **Settings > Organization**.: A **CA certificate** that you generate and [register on the tunnel](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#add-a-ca-certificate). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel
- [parameter] **Domain**: Copy the assigned `abcd1234.tunnel.anthropic.com` value. Your proxy's routes are subdomains of this domain. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#get-the-connection-details
- [parameter] **Token**: Click the eye icon (**Show token**) to fetch the tunnel token, then use the copy icon to copy it into your tunnel stack's secret store. Click **Rotate token** to invalidate the current token and issue a new one. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#get-the-connection-details
- [definition] Open the MCP tunnels page — In the Console sidebar, go to **Manage > MCP tunnels**. Tunnels are workspace-scoped; the new tunnel belongs to the workspace currently selected in the Console, so switch workspaces first if you want it elsewhere. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel
- [definition] Name the tunnel — Click **New tunnel** and enter a name in the **Create tunnel** dialog. The name is required and identifies the tunnel in the list, on the detail page, and in the agent MCP server picker. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel
- [definition] Optionally set up programmatic access — If your role can manage federation rules, a **Set up programmatic access** toggle appears (off by default). If not, the Console shows a notice in its place and your tunnel stack uses the manual flow instead. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel
- [definition] Create the tunnel — Click **Create tunnel**. The Console provisions the tunnel and opens the detail page. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#create-a-tunnel
- [definition] Get the connection details — Open the tunnel. The detail page shows a **Connection** section with the domain and token and a **Certificates** section. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#get-the-connection-details
- [definition] Add a CA certificate — Anthropic verifies [inner TLS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) to your [proxy](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) against the CA certificates you register on the tunnel. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#add-a-ca-certificate
- [definition] Find the Certificates section — On the tunnel's detail page, scroll to the **Certificates** section and click **Add certificate**. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#add-a-ca-certificate
- [definition] Provide the certificate — Click **Choose file** to select a `.pem`, `.crt`, or `.cer` file, drag the file onto the text area, or paste the PEM block directly. The modal rejects private-key material and content that isn't a `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` block. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#add-a-ca-certificate
- [definition] Add the certificate — Click **Add certificate**. The fingerprint and expiry appear in the certificate list, and the slot count on the section header increments. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#add-a-ca-certificate
- [definition] Deploy the tunnel stack — The tunnel exists in the Console, but no traffic flows until the tunnel stack is running inside your network and dialed in with the tunnel token. Follow one of the deploy guides: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#deploy-the-tunnel-stack
- [definition] Use the tunnel in an agent — Once your stack is running and has one or more MCP servers configured, attach an upstream MCP server to a Managed Agent session. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#use-the-tunnel-in-an-agent
- [definition] Open the New session modal — Go to **Managed Agents > Sessions** and click **New session**. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#use-the-tunnel-in-an-agent
- [definition] Define an inline agent — In the agent picker, choose **Create new agent** so you can edit the MCP server list directly. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#use-the-tunnel-in-an-agent
- [definition] Add the MCP server — Click **+ MCP Server** and open the dropdown. Tunnels created in the current workspace appear at the top of the list, above the public connector catalog. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#use-the-tunnel-in-an-agent
- [definition] Supply the routing — The card shows two optional fields: **Subdomain** (prefixed to the tunnel domain) and **Path** (appended after it). Fill in one or both, depending on how your proxy's routes are configured. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#use-the-tunnel-in-an-agent
- [definition] Archive a tunnel — Archiving immediately stops the tunnel from accepting connections and is permanent. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#archive-a-tunnel

- [parameter] `authorization_token`: Type=string; Required=No; Description=OAuth authorization token if required by the MCP server. See [Authentication](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#authentication) for how to obtain one, or the [MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization) for protocol details. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#field-descriptions
- [parameter] `type`: Type=string; Required=Yes; Description=Must be "mcp\_toolset". — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#field-descriptions
- [parameter] `mcp_server_name`: Type=string; Required=Yes; Description=Must match a server name defined in the `mcp_servers` array. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#field-descriptions
- [parameter] `default_config`: Type=object; Required=No; Description=Default configuration applied to all tools in this set. Individual tool configs in `configs` override these defaults. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#field-descriptions
- [parameter] `configs`: Type=object; Required=No; Description=Per-tool configuration overrides. Keys are tool names, values are configuration objects. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#field-descriptions
- [parameter] `cache_control`: Type=object; Required=No; Description=[Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) cache breakpoint configuration for this toolset. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#field-descriptions
- [parameter] `enabled`: Type=boolean; Default=`true`; Description=Whether this tool is enabled. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#tool-configuration-options
- [parameter] `defer_loading`: Type=boolean; Default=`false`; Description=If true, tool description is not sent to the model initially. Used with [Tool search tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#tool-configuration-options
- [parameter] `mcpTools(tools, mcpClient)`: Converts MCP tools to Claude API tools for use with `client.beta.messages.toolRunner()` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#available-helpers
- [parameter] `mcpMessages(messages)`: Converts MCP prompt messages to Claude API message format — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#available-helpers
- [parameter] `mcpResourceToContent(resource)`: Converts an MCP resource to a Claude API content block — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#available-helpers
- [parameter] `mcpResourceToFile(resource)`: Converts an MCP resource to a file object for upload — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#available-helpers
- [parameter] No `tool_configuration` (all tools enabled): MCPToolset with no `default_config` or `configs` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#common-migration-patterns
- [parameter] `tool_configuration.enabled: false`: MCPToolset with `default_config.enabled: false` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#common-migration-patterns
- [parameter] `tool_configuration.allowed_tools: [...]`: MCPToolset with `default_config.enabled: false` and specific tools enabled in `configs` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#common-migration-patterns

- [parameter] `tool_configuration.enabled`: Type=boolean; Description=**Deprecated:** Use `default_config.enabled` in MCPToolset — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#deprecated-field-descriptions
- [parameter] `tool_configuration.allowed_tools`: Type=array; Description=**Deprecated:** Use allowlist pattern with `configs` in MCPToolset — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#deprecated-field-descriptions
- [definition] When Claude uses MCP tools — Once an MCP server is connected, Claude calls its tools when the user's request maps to a tool's described capability, either explicitly ("search Jira for open bugs") or implicitly ("what's blocking the release?" with a Jira server attached). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#when-claude-uses-mcp-tools
- [definition] Basic example — This example enables all tools from an MCP server with default configuration: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#basic-example
- [definition] MCP server configuration — Each MCP server in the `mcp_servers` array defines the connection details: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#mcp-server-configuration
- [definition] MCP toolset configuration — The MCPToolset lives in the `tools` array and configures which tools from the MCP server are enabled and how they should be configured. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#mcp-toolset-configuration
- [definition] Tool configuration options — Each tool (whether configured in `default_config` or in `configs`) supports the following fields: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#tool-configuration-options
- [definition] Configuration merging — Configuration values merge with this precedence (highest to lowest): — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#configuration-merging
- [definition] Enable all tools with default configuration — The simplest pattern: enable all tools from a server: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#enable-all-tools-with-default-configuration
- [definition] Allowlist: enable only specific tools — Set `enabled: false` as the default, then explicitly enable specific tools: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#allowlist-enable-only-specific-tools
- [definition] Denylist: disable specific tools — Enable all tools by default, then explicitly disable unwanted tools. Denylisting write or destructive tools is recommended when building read-only assistants, or when you want a human confirmation step before state changes: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#denylist-disable-specific-tools
- [definition] Mixed: allowlist with per-tool configuration — Combine allowlisting with custom configuration for each tool: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#mixed-allowlist-with-per-tool-configuration
- [definition] Validation rules — The API enforces these validation rules: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#validation-rules
- [definition] Response content types — When Claude uses MCP tools, the response includes two new content block types: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#response-content-types
- [definition] Multiple MCP servers — You can connect to multiple MCP servers by including multiple server definitions in `mcp_servers` and a corresponding MCPToolset for each in the `tools` array: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#multiple-mcp-servers
- [definition] Authentication — For MCP servers that require OAuth authentication, you'll need to obtain an access token. The MCP connector beta supports passing an `authorization_token` parameter in the MCP server definition. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#authentication
- [definition] Obtaining an access token for testing — The MCP inspector can guide you through the process of obtaining an access token for testing purposes. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#obtaining-an-access-token-for-testing
- [definition] Using the access token — Once you've obtained an access token using either of the preceding OAuth flows, you can use it in your MCP server configuration: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#using-the-access-token
- [definition] Client-side MCP helpers — If you manage your own MCP client connection (for example, with local stdio servers, MCP prompts, or MCP resources), the SDKs provide helper functions that convert between MCP types and Claude API types. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#client-side-mcp-helpers
- [definition] Installation — Install both the Anthropic SDK and the MCP SDK: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#installation
- [definition] Use MCP tools — Convert MCP tools for use with the SDK's [tool runner](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-runner), which handles tool execution automatically: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#use-mcp-tools
- [definition] Use MCP prompts — Convert MCP prompt messages into Claude API message format: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#use-mcp-prompts
- [definition] Use MCP resources — Convert MCP resources into content blocks to include in messages, or into file objects for upload: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#use-mcp-resources
- [definition] Error handling — The conversion functions throw `UnsupportedMCPValueError` if an MCP value isn't supported by the Claude API (in Go, the helpers return an `UnsupportedValueError`; in Java and C#, they throw `AnthropicInvalidDataException`). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#error-handling
- [definition] Batch requests — You can include `mcp_servers` in [Message Batches API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) requests. MCP tool calls through the Batches API are priced the same as those in regular Messages API requests. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#batch-requests
- [definition] Data retention — The MCP connector is not covered by ZDR arrangements. Data exchanged with MCP servers, including tool definitions and execution results, is retained according to Anthropic's standard data retention policy. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#data-retention
- [definition] Migration guide — If you're using the deprecated `mcp-client-2025-04-04` beta header, follow this guide to migrate to the new version. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#migration-guide
- [definition] Key changes — 1. **New beta header:** Change from `mcp-client-2025-04-04` to `mcp-client-2025-11-20` 2. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#key-changes
- [definition] Deprecated version: mcp-client-2025-04-04 — This version is deprecated. Migrate to `mcp-client-2025-11-20` using the preceding [migration guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#migration-guide). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector#deprecated-version-mcp-client-2025-04-04

- [parameter] `log_level`: Description=Logging verbosity: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, or `error`.; Default=`info` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `shutdown_timeout`: Description=How long to wait for in-flight requests during graceful shutdown.; Default=`30s` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `tunnel_domain`: Description=Base domain assigned to the tunnel. When set, route lookup strips this suffix from incoming hostnames so `routes` keys can be bare subdomains (`wiki`). When empty, `routes` keys must be exact full hostnames.; Default=Required when `routes` keys are bare subdomains — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `tls.cert_file`: Description=Path to the server TLS certificate.; Default=Required — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `tls.key_file`: Description=Path to the server TLS private key.; Default=Required — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `routes`: Description=Map of subdomain or full hostname to upstream URL. See [Route matching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#route-matching).; Default=Required — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `upstream.allowed_ips`: Description=IPv4 CIDR ranges or single addresses the proxy is permitted to connect to. Mutually exclusive with `disable_ip_validation`.; Default=RFC1918 private ranges — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `upstream.disable_ip_validation`: Description=Disable upstream IP validation entirely. Mutually exclusive with `allowed_ips`.; Default=`false` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `upstream.tls.ca_file`: Description=CA bundle for validating upstream TLS.; Default=None — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `upstream.tls.include_system_cas`: Description=Also trust the system CA bundle for upstream TLS.; Default=`false` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [parameter] `Authorization`: `Bearer <token>` (the WIF-exchanged token) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#tunnels-api
- [parameter] `anthropic-version`: `2023-06-01` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#tunnels-api
- [parameter] `anthropic-beta`: `mcp-tunnels-2026-06-22` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#tunnels-api
- [parameter] `--api-url`: Description=Claude API base URL. Also read from `API_URL`.; Default=Required — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-init
- [parameter] `--tunnel-id`: Description=Tunnel ID to attach to (`tnl_...`). Also read from `TUNNEL_ID`. When omitted, a new tunnel is created; a tunnel ID already stored in the output is reused on re-runs.; Default=None (create a tunnel) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-init
- [parameter] `--output`: Description=Output destination: `dir:/path` or `k8s-secret:NAME`. The Helm chart passes `k8s-secret:<release>`.; Default=`k8s-secret:mcp-tunnel` (auto-detected when running in a Kubernetes pod; required otherwise) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-init
- [parameter] `--cert-duration`: Description=Server certificate validity period.; Default=`2160h` (90 days) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-init
- [parameter] `--token-version`: Description=Change-detection string. A new value triggers token rotation on re-run. The Helm chart and the Compose example both pass `1` as the initial value.; Default=None — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-init
- [parameter] `--output`: Description=Output destination: `dir:/path` or `k8s-secret:NAME`. The Helm chart passes `k8s-secret:<release>`.; Default=`k8s-secret:mcp-tunnel` (auto-detected when running in a Kubernetes pod; required otherwise) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-renew-cert
- [parameter] `--cert-duration`: Description=New certificate validity period.; Default=`2160h` (90 days) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-renew-cert
- [parameter] `--renew-before`: Description=Skip renewal if the existing certificate has more than this duration remaining.; Default=`0` (always renew) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-renew-cert
- [definition] Proxy configuration — The [proxy](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) reads its configuration from `/etc/mcp-gateway/config.yaml` (Compose) or the rendered ConfigMap (Helm, populated from `gateway.config.*`). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration
- [definition] Route matching — `routes` is a flat string map (`map[string]string`), not a list. The proxy looks up the incoming hostname by exact match first, then by stripping the `tunnel_domain` suffix and matching the remaining subdomain. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#route-matching
- [definition] Tunnels API — The Tunnels REST API lives at `/v1/tunnels` and supports creating, listing, and archiving tunnels, registering CA certificates, and revealing or rotating the tunnel token. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#tunnels-api
- [definition] Certificate requirements — The [setup component](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components) generates compliant certificates automatically. These requirements apply only if you issue certificates through your own PKI. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#certificate-requirements
- [definition] CA certificate — Upload with `POST /v1/tunnels/{tunnel_id}/certificates`. A tunnel can hold up to two active CA certificates at a time, which allows zero-downtime rotation. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#ca-certificate
- [definition] Server certificate — Presented by the proxy during [inner TLS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/concepts#components). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#server-certificate
- [definition] Setup component — The setup component ships inside the `mcp-proxy` image as the `setup` binary. Run it with `docker compose run --rm setup <subcommand>` (Compose) or rely on the chart's hooks and CronJobs (Helm). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-component
- [definition] `setup init` — Attaches to an existing tunnel (or creates one when no tunnel ID is supplied), then generates a CA and server certificate, registers the CA, retrieves the tunnel token, and writes all outputs to the destination. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-init
- [definition] `setup renew-cert` — Issues a new server certificate signed by the stored CA. Makes no API calls. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#setup-renew-cert

## Best practices
<https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security>

- [snippet] Stop the tunnel stack: helm uninstall mcp-tunnel -n mcp-tunnel — `helm uninstall mcp-tunnel -n mcp-tunnel` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [snippet] Stop the tunnel stack: docker compose down --timeout 0 — `docker compose down --timeout 0` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [snippet] Stop the tunnel stack: helm uninstall mcp-tunnel -n mcp-tunnel — `helm uninstall mcp-tunnel -n mcp-tunnel` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#tear-down-a-tunnel
- [snippet] Stop the tunnel stack: docker compose down — `docker compose down` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#tear-down-a-tunnel
- [snippet] Remove stored credentials: kubectl -n mcp-tunnel delete secret \ — `kubectl -n mcp-tunnel delete secret \` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#tear-down-a-tunnel
- [snippet] Remove stored credentials: sudo rm -rf data — `sudo rm -rf data` — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#tear-down-a-tunnel
- [definition] Respond to a suspected breach — If you believe your tunnel token, TLS keys, or proxy host has been compromised: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [definition] Detach the upstream MCP servers — Remove the upstream MCP servers from any Managed Agent sessions that use them, and stop passing their URLs in the `mcp_servers` block of Messages API requests. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [definition] Archive the tunnel — Archiving invalidates the tunnel token and detaches the domain. In the Console, [archive the tunnel](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#archive-a-tunnel) from the **MCP tunnels** list. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [definition] Contact Anthropic — Report the suspected compromise to Anthropic support. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [definition] Rotate downstream credentials — Re-provision a fresh tunnel and rotate any OAuth tokens that the affected MCP servers issued. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [definition] Review logs before restoring service — Inspect proxy, cloudflared, and MCP server logs for the window of suspected compromise before bringing the new tunnel online. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#respond-to-a-suspected-breach
- [definition] Tear down a tunnel — Follow these steps to decommission a tunnel and remove all stored credentials. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#tear-down-a-tunnel
- [definition] Archive the tunnel — In the Console, [archive the tunnel](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/console#archive-a-tunnel) from the **MCP tunnels** list. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security#tear-down-a-tunnel

- [definition] How it works — When the memory tool is enabled, Claude automatically checks its memory directory before starting a task. As it works, Claude stores what it learns in files under `/memories` and reads them back in later conversations to continue earlier work. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#how-it-works
- [definition] Implement the memory handler — Claude's reply to a request like the previous one ends with a `tool_use` block that requests a memory operation, such as `view /memories`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#implement-the-memory-handler
- [definition] Tool commands — Your client-side implementation must handle the following commands. These specifications describe the recommended behaviors and return strings: Claude reads whatever text your tool result contains, so you can return different strings if your application needs to. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#tool-commands
- [definition] view — Shows directory contents or file contents with optional line ranges: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#view
- [definition] Prompting guidance — When the memory tool is present in your request's `tools`, the API automatically adds this instruction to the system prompt. You don't need to send it yourself: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#prompting-guidance
- [definition] Security considerations — Your application executes every file operation Claude requests, so these safeguards are your responsibility: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#security-considerations
- [definition] Sensitive information — Claude usually refuses to write sensitive information to memory files. For stronger guarantees, add validation that strips sensitive data before your handler writes the file. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#sensitive-information
- [definition] File storage size — Track memory file sizes and cap how large a file can grow. Consider capping how many characters the `view` command returns, and let Claude page through the rest with `view_range`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#file-storage-size
- [definition] Memory expiration — Periodically delete memory files that haven't been accessed in a long time. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#memory-expiration
- [definition] Path traversal protection — A malicious path such as `/memories/../../secrets.env` can reach files outside the `/memories` directory. Your implementation must validate every path in every command to prevent directory traversal attacks. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#path-traversal-protection
- [definition] Error handling — The memory tool uses similar error-handling patterns to the [text editor tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/text-editor-tool#handle-errors). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#error-handling
- [definition] Context editing integration — The memory tool pairs with context editing to manage long-running conversations. For details, see [Context editing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing). — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#context-editing-integration
- [definition] Using with compaction — The memory tool can also be paired with [compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction), which summarizes older conversation context server-side. Context editing clears specific tool results on the client. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#using-with-compaction
- [definition] Multisession software development pattern — For software projects that span multiple agent sessions, set up memory files deliberately instead of writing them ad hoc as work progresses. The following pattern turns memory into a recovery mechanism: each new session resumes from the state the last one recorded. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#multisession-software-development-pattern
- [definition] How the pattern works — 1. **Initializer session:** The first session sets up the memory files before any substantive work begins. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#how-the-pattern-works
- [definition] Key principle — Work on one feature at a time. Mark a feature complete only after end-to-end verification confirms it works, not when the code is written. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool#key-principle

- [definition] Mid-conversation tool changes — The `tools` array sits even earlier in the hashed request prefix than the top-level `system` field, so editing it invalidates the [prompt cache](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) for the entire conversation. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#mid-conversation-tool-changes
- [definition] When to use a mid-conversation system message — [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) hashes the request prefix in order: `tools`, then `system`, then `messages`. A cache hit requires the prefix to match a recent request exactly, byte for byte, up to the cache breakpoint. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#when-to-use-a-mid-conversation-system-message
- [definition] How it works — Add a message with `"role": "system"` to the `messages` array. Use a plain string or content blocks for `content`, the same as a `user` or `assistant` turn. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#how-it-works
- [definition] Placement after tool results — In an [agentic loop](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview), the system message goes after the `user` message that delivers the tool results. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#placement-after-tool-results
- [definition] Combining with prompt caching — Mid-conversation system messages and [prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) are designed to be used together: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#combining-with-prompt-caching

- [definition] Execution semantics — When Claude calls tools, the response has a `stop_reason` of `tool_use` and can contain several `tool_use` blocks in a single assistant turn. How you run those calls is your decision. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use#execution-semantics
- [definition] Maximizing parallel tool use — Claude 4 and later models make parallel tool calls by default when a request benefits from multiple tools. For all models, you can increase the likelihood of parallel tool calls with targeted prompting: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use#maximizing-parallel-tool-use
- [definition] Disable parallel tool use — Parallel tool use is on by default. To turn it off, set `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` inside the [`tool_choice`](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools#forcing-tool-use) object. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use#disable-parallel-tool-use
- [definition] At most one tool call — When `tool_choice` type is `auto` (the default), setting `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` means Claude calls at most one tool per response. Claude can still answer in plain text without calling any tool. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use#at-most-one-tool-call
- [definition] Exactly one tool call — When `tool_choice` type is `any` or `tool`, setting `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` means Claude calls exactly one tool. The following example uses `any`. — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use#exactly-one-tool-call
- [definition] Troubleshooting — If Claude isn't making parallel tool calls when expected, check these common issues: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use#troubleshooting

- [definition] How programmatic tool calling works — When you configure a tool to be callable from code execution and Claude determines that tool is needed: — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/programmatic-tool-calling#how-programmatic-tool-calling-works
